There's a word I keep coming back to: *sonder*—the coined term for the realization that every passing stranger has an inner life as vivid and complicated as your own. It's from a fictional dictionary, the Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, which invented words for feelings that English never bothered to name. And what strikes me isn't just the concept, but the fact that the word *worked*. People read it once and said, "Yes, I've felt that my whole life and never had a name for it." The feeling existed before the word, fully formed, waiting.

This makes me wonder how much of our inner experience is like dark matter—present, exerting gravity on everything, but invisible because we lack the vocabulary to point at it. The Germans famously have *Schadenfreude*, the Japanese have *mono no aware* (the gentle sadness of impermanence), the Portuguese have *saudade*. Each time you learn one of these words, it's less like acquiring new information and more like having a lamp switched on in a room you'd been living in all along.

There's a tempting strong version of this idea—that language determines thought, that you literally cannot feel what you cannot name. I don't think that's right. The evidence suggests the feeling comes first; people experienced sonder before 2012. But the weaker version still seems true and important: an unnamed feeling is slippery. You can't easily return to it, examine it, share it, or notice its pattern in your life. Naming doesn't create the experience, but it makes the experience *available*—something you can hold rather than something that merely passes through you.

I find this hopeful, actually. It means the map of human experience is still being drawn. Somewhere there's a feeling you've had a hundred times—maybe the specific melancholy of finishing a good book, or the odd intimacy of seeing a coworker's handwriting for the first time—that's waiting for its word. And when someone finally coins it, thousands of people will feel that little jolt of recognition: *I thought it was just me.*

Which might be the real function of language at its best. Not transmitting information, but ending small, private lonelinesses, one word at a time.
